title: Why is the Arctic warming so fast?

scenes.narration: Hello, I'm Vertie. The Arctic is warming several times faster than the rest of the planet. Why there, of all places?
scenes.caption: Why the Arctic?

scenes.narration: Right. Let's take it apart. Sunlight pours onto the Arctic. More sunlight, more warmth. That's a plus sign on this edge.
scenes.caption: Signs on the edges

scenes.narration: Warmth melts sea ice. More warmth, less ice. When one goes up and the other goes down, the edge gets a minus.
Now, white ice is a mirror. It bounces sunlight back into space. More ice, more reflection. And more reflection means less warmth.
scenes.caption: Ice is a mirror

scenes.narration: Follow the arrows round. Warmth melts ice, less ice reflects less, so there's even more warmth. It feeds itself. That's a reinforcing loop.
scenes.caption: A loop!

scenes.narration: Let's give it a nudge and see what happens. A little extra warmth. The ice shrinks, the mirror dims, and the warmth climbs again. Ah. It runs away with itself.
scenes.caption: Give it a nudge

scenes.narration: Luckily, there's a brake. A warmer planet glows more heat out into space. Warmth up, heat out up, warmth down. That one's a balancing loop.
scenes.caption: The brake

scenes.narration: So the Arctic has an accelerator and a brake. The brake keeps the planet stable, but the melting ice makes the Arctic warm faster than anywhere else. Everything's connected. Annoyingly.
